newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: SE Asian Grain-Malaysian corn down as supply rises.
newsitem.headline: SE Asian Grain-Malaysian corn down as supply rises.

text.p: Domestic Malaysian corn prices have been hit by mounting supply and aggressive selling over the past week, while corn quotes in other regional markets were steady to firmer, traders said on Wednesday.
"Prices have been on a downward trend mainly because there are a lot of goods in the market," one Malaysian trader said.
"It's difficult to find storage space, so suppliers are selling in the shortest possible time before arrival of new shipments," he said.
With few shipments of imported U.S. corn expected this month, traders said local prices would remain under pressure.
The price of bulk corn, ex-factory/godown in Malaysia's central region, was at 395 ringgit ($158) a tonne, compared with 400-410 ringgit a week ago.
"Prices won't be good for February at least. Price recovery, if any, can only be seen in March," said another trader.
At 395 ringgit, he said, suppliers were selling at a loss. "You need to sell at 410-420 ringgit to break even," he said.
Traders said there could be some buying after the Chinese New Year and Moslem Eid al-Fitr festivities this week, but there were ample supplies to meet the demand.
They added that most buyers were covered until March. Malaysia was reported to have purchased up to 100,000 tonnes of corn for February and March deliveries with the bulk of the imports from China.

"A" grade wheat in bags, ex-factory/godown in the central region, continued to fetch about 800 ringgit a tonne FOB, while the price of low-grade wheat also remained at around 450 ringgit a tonne FOB, both in the central region.

In Indonesia, traders said they expect corn supplies to be adequate to meet domestic demand with the start of the harvest this month in six provinces, including the key producing area of Lampung in South Sumatra, and recent large imports.
"We expect corn to continue to flood in from Lampung because of the harvest. The harvest will last through May, but it will reach its peak in February and March," said one Lampung trader.
Government officials have said that some 351,000 hectares planted with a high-yielding hybrid strain is expected to be harvested from January through until March.
Traders said around 220,000 tonnes of mostly U.S. corn arrived in Indonesia last week.
One trader in Jakarta said offers from China had started to come to the market but no deals had been done yet because levels were higher than U.S.-origin offers.

"China has been offering corn at $148-$153 a tonne C&F for February to March shipment, but no deals have been done," the trader said, adding that Argentine-origin corn was being offered at $145 a tonne C&F.
One trader said there was some expectation that Indonesia might export corn to Malaysia this year because supplies are projected to be high in the wake of the harvest.
"We can even export corn if we want to do it now, the problem is that our price still cannot compete with those of China."
Traders said domestic soymeal prices were a touch easier after recent firm levels which reflected strong feedmill demand ahead of the Eid al-Fitr moslem festival this week.
Soymeal was quoted at 785-790 rupiah a kg in Jakarta compared with 795-800 rupiah a week ago.
One trader said Indonesian feedmills had bought about 175,000 tonnes of soymeal in January at about $337-$340 a tonne, with about 70 percent of the meal coming from local suppliers.
In Thailand, the animal feed industry remains uninterested in Chinese corn preferring U.S. origin, industry sources said.

Ample local supplies and the high tariff imposed on Chinese corn has sidelined Thai buyers who said they would hold back from the market until the government announces a new schedule for zero-tariff corn imports.
"We are in no rush. Even though we want to import some now, we do not find the $150 per tonne offered by China exceedingly exciting," said one local feed producer.
Corn imports from China, which is not a member of the World Trade Organization (WTO), are subject to six percent tariff plus a surcharge of 1,000 baht ($38.46) a tonne.

The industry, however, had mixed views on when they would need to import corn. While some think local supplies will be adequate until April, others believed the government will need to open zero-tariff corn imports soon after the Chinese New Year holiday this week.
